task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: Defensive suppression of opponent second-half minus first-half (H2-H1) change
Opponent halftime adjustment and counter strategy
Regression to the mean and game-flow mechanics in H2-H1 differences
methodological_questions: Is a team defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across split halves of a season and across seasons?
What is the noise floor for a per-team-season H2-H1 mean with about 120 team-seasons?
How can opponent quality, score state, garbage time, rotation and regression to the mean be separated from a defensive trait?
Is H2-H1 change a mechanical product of game flow rather than a defensive trait?

historical_evidence.finding: Connector teammate-path quality Q_p (a player-season on-off PPP gap) had split-half r=+0.215, Spearman-Brown ~0.355 and ICC 0.216 (78.4% within-player variance), with n=102. [prior work] says this is too low to treat as a stable scoutable trait. It was limited by low measurement reliability (RISK:MEASURE_RELIABILITY).

Inferred defensive-scheme change labels showed change in 61.0% of within-game cells and 67.7% of cross-game pairs, with near-uniform transition matrices. [prior work]'s caveat is that the inferred label cannot separate real defensive adjustment from the offense executing differently, and the pattern is consistent with label noise (RISK:LABEL_ERROR).

Season stability of each star's top sequential suppressor was low: only 2/30 (7%) met the 75% same-top-suppressor rule. It was recorded as an adequately powered null (B_powered_null), with small cells (min n=20).

For BEST counters, 64/78 (82%) of (offense, play type) cells had more than one oracle player across opponents. [prior work] reads this as matchup specificity rather than a single stable team identity.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating an on-off derived quantity as a stable attribute
failed_approaches.why: Low measurement reliability: most variance is within-unit from one half to the other ([prior work]).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive adjustment from labels derived from play-by-play
failed_approaches.why: Label or classification error; real adjustment cannot be separated from the offense executing differently ([prior work]).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Assuming a stable suppressor identity across seasons
failed_approaches.why: Powered null; only 2/30 stable, with small cells ([prior work]).

evidence_establishes: In this project, related derived defensive or on-off traits have shown low split-half or season-to-season stability ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Inferred defensive-adjustment labels are noisy and cannot be read as real adjustment ([prior work][prior work]).
Defensive suppression effects appear to be specific to the opponent matchup rather than a single fixed team identity ([prior work][prior work], as recorded for BEST counters).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record measures a team defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change, nor its reliability.
No retrieved record gives a noise floor, a regression-to-the-mean estimate or a garbage-time treatment for H2-H1 metrics.
The related null and low-reliability results concern different constructs (players, play-type suppressors, scheme labels) and do not transfer directly to team-level H2-H1.
own_inferences: H2-H1 is a difference of two noisy half-game scores. Per-game SD is plausibly around 10-12 points, so a 41-game half-season mean has an SE near 1.7-2 points. Any true team-level SD is probably well under 1 point, so I expect split-half reliability near zero to low.

A defense that suppresses H1 scoring mechanically raises expected H2-H1 through regression to the mean. Any H2-H1 effect must be separated from H1 level and from score-state effects such as garbage time, starter minutes and opponent adjustment.

If the H2-H1 effect is mostly the opponent's own adjustment or rotation pattern, then 'defense effect' is misattributed. Opponent-adjusted estimates should be used, and the effect partly reflects offense.

With about 120 team-seasons (likely 4 regular seasons x 30), a split-half correlation test has roughly 80% power for true r≈0.25, but little power for smaller values. A null would therefore only rule out moderate reliability.
Season-to-season pairs (about 90) are not independent because the same team appears more than once, so the effective sample size is smaller.
uncertainties: The exact definition of the H2-H1 metric (points, PPP or efficiency, and whether it is possession-adjusted) is not given.
It is unclear whether the 120 units are regular-season only. Playoff team-seasons would be too small and unbalanced to use.
It is unknown how much of the effect is a stable defensive trait versus coaching or roster change across seasons.
The matchup-minute data are only partial possessions, so they may not support attribution to specific defenders.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records show that derived defensive traits repeatedly fail reliability checks, and that scheme inference is label-noisy. This lowered my expected probability of 'supported', led me to make reliability the primary endpoint with split-half, Spearman-Brown and ICC estimates, and to avoid scheme labels. It did not change the basic decision to run a narrow test.

blocking_constraints.text: Per-team H2-H1 means are dominated by game-level noise. Low observed reliability is the likely finding, and it is also the question's own estimand.
Only 120 team-seasons. Power is adequate only for moderate reliability (about r≥0.25), so a null cannot exclude small stable effects.
H2-H1 is mechanically coupled to H1 level, so regression to the mean must be modeled.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests team-level H2-H1 suppression reliability directly. Related project work on player-level and play-type-level defensive traits found low reliability or instability, which makes a low-reliability finding likely here.

risks.text: Difference scores have low reliability, since the variance of a difference sums the two halves' noise. Report split-half, Spearman-Brown and ICC with confidence intervals.
Defenses strong in H1 will show a higher H2-H1 change by regression. Control for H1 opponent expected points and use odd/even game splits to avoid selection on the outcome.
Opponent quality, home/away, pace, foul trouble, starter minutes, score state and garbage time all drive H2-H1. Opponent adjustment and a team's own offense are needed.
120 units gives limited power for small reliabilities. Consecutive-season pairs are clustered by team.
Roster, coaching and league-wide scoring trends change across 2022-23 to 2025-26, so season-to-season stability confounds trait stability with roster change.
Blowouts and clock management alter H2 possessions mechanically. Exclude or winsorize games by margin and use a possession-based metric.
Any adjustment for H1 or H2 outcomes must be computed in the held-out half only. Do not use full-season team quality estimated from the same games.
The reliability estimate needs a permutation benchmark, with opponents' H2-H1 change shuffled across teams within game types.

design.estimand: Reliability (split-half correlation with Spearman-Brown correction, plus variance-component ICC) of a team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change in points per 100 possessions. The effect is opponent-adjusted and H1-level-adjusted. A secondary estimand is the season-to-season correlation of the same quantity.
design.unit: Team-season (regular season), with game-level observations nested within it.
design.sample: The 120 regular-season team-seasons from 2022-23 to 2025-26, using games complete as of the frozen data date. Exclude playoffs from the primary analysis (too few games per team). Exclude games with an H1 margin above 25 and possessions in H2 after garbage-time rules, with a sensitivity analysis including them.
design.power: For n=120 and a two-sided alpha of 0.05, power is about 0.80 for true r=0.25. Detectable reliability below about 0.25 is not claimed. Use a game-level mixed model (opponent, home/away, rest and H1 expected points as covariates, with a random team intercept) to get the ICC and bootstrap CIs, resampling teams. For season-to-season stability use cluster bootstrap by team over the 90 consecutive-season pairs.
design.controls: Opponent offensive strength (computed excluding the focal game), home/away, rest, pace, H1 margin and H1 opponent efficiency (regression to the mean), garbage-time exclusion, starter minutes in H2, and injuries or lineup availability where available. Split by odd/even game number, with a second split by random game permutation (1,000 repeats). Estimate the control model on the training split only.
design.falsification: Permutation benchmark: shuffle opponents' H2-H1 changes across teams within game-type strata, and repeat the split-half analysis to get the null distribution of r. Also run a negative-control outcome (opponent H2-H1 change in a statistic unrelated to defense, such as free-throw rate on early shots) and an H1-only versus H2-only reliability comparison. If H1 and H2 effects are each reliable but H2-H1 is not, the trait is level, not change.
design.multiplicity: One primary endpoint (split-half Spearman-Brown reliability for the primary metric). Secondary: season-to-season correlation, ICC, and one sensitivity per garbage-time rule, controlled with Holm correction. No other metrics or subgroup cuts are claimed confirmatory.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the Spearman-Brown reliability is at least 0.50 with the lower 95% bootstrap bound above 0.30, the result beats the permutation null (p<0.01), and the season-to-season correlation is positive with a lower bound above 0. Rejected if the upper 95% bound on the split-half r is below 0.25 and the ICC upper bound is below 0.10. Anything else is reported as inconclusive. If the result survives only without RTM and garbage-time control, report it as an artifact.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files for 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons, frozen at the 2026-10-06 data snapshot (2025-26 complete from 2026-04-13). Record the file hashes and the possession-reconstruction code version before any analysis.
